hero.headline: Looking for something to do Halloween weekend? Here are the Top 5 local events for Oct. 30-Nov. 1
hero.teaser: A free Port St. Lucie fall festival, Halloween fun with wildlife in Hobe Sound, live music in Fort Pierce and Vero Beach, and a classic car show in Stuart lead this weekend's picks.
hero.body:
Halloween falls on Saturday this year, and the Treasure Coast has plenty happening from Friday evening through Sunday. Families can kick off the weekend with carnival rides and trick-or-treating in Port St. Lucie or get a closer look at animal ambassadors in Hobe Sound. Saturday offers a Halloween-themed Blues Brothers tribute in Fort Pierce and an eclectic live-music set in Vero Beach, while Sunday brings a vintage car show to downtown Stuart.

 Here are five standout events for Friday evening, Oct. 30, Saturday, Oct. 31, and Sunday, Nov. 1 , across Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties.

 1. Fall Fun Fest, Port St. Lucie

 When: Friday, Oct. 30, 5-10 p.m. Where: MIDFLORIDA Event Center, 9221 SE Event Center Place, Port St. Lucie. Admission: Free; check with the organizer about individual attractions and purchases.

 The MIDFLORIDA Event Center's Fall Fun Fest opens the weekend with live music, carnival rides, food, family activities and trick-or-treating. The organizer describes it as a three-day event, making this a centerpiece of the Halloween weekend calendar.

 The confirmed Friday hours are 5-10 p.m.; check the event center's listing for the schedules on its other dates and any costs beyond general admission. Festival details .

 2. Creepy Creature Feature, Hobe Sound

 When: Friday, Oct. 30, 5:30-7:30 p.m. Where: Hobe Sound Nature Center, 13640 SE Federal Highway, Hobe Sound. Admission: Not specified in the calendar; confirm with the organizer.

 The Hobe Sound Nature Center brings back its family-friendly Creepy Creature Feature for a wildlife-themed Halloween evening. The event listing highlights glitter tattoos and the center's animal ambassadors among the attractions.

 It's a seasonal option for families who would rather spend part of Halloween weekend meeting animals than attending a conventional costume party. Check the organizer for participation details before going. Event details .

 3. Jake and Elwood Blues Revue and Halloween look-alike contest, Fort Pierce

 When: Saturday, Oct. 31, 1-4 p.m.; look-alike contest listed for 3 p.m. Where: Summer Crush Vineyard & Winery, 4200 Johnston Road, Fort Pierce. Admission: $18.50 listed in the TCT events calendar; confirm current ticket terms with the organizer.

 A six-piece Blues Brothers tribute act takes the stage at Summer Crush Vineyard & Winery for a Halloween afternoon of music. The listing also advertises a Jake-and-Elwood-style look-alike contest at 3 p.m., giving visitors a reason to work the duo's signature look into their costumes.

 For anyone seeking live entertainment rather than a traditional trick-or-treating outing, this combines a concert with a holiday costume competition. Show details .

 4. Hot Sauce Moon at Riverside Theatre, Vero Beach

 When: Saturday, Oct. 31, 5:30-8:30 p.m. Where: Riverside Theatre, 3250 Riverside Park Drive, Vero Beach. Admission: Not specified in the calendar; check the venue.

 Hot Sauce Moon provides an Indian River County option for Halloween night. Riverside Theatre describes the band's sound as an eclectic mix of classic rock, folk rock, country and blues, with the performance listed on its Loop Music Calendar.

 The evening set is an alternative for readers who want to hear live music after daytime Halloween activities. Verify seating and admission arrangements with Riverside Theatre. Music calendar .

 5. Cars of Our Lives Show, Stuart

 When: Sunday, Nov. 1, 9 a.m.-3 p.m. Where: City of Stuart Water Tower, 301 SE Stypmann Boulevard, Stuart. Admission: Free.

 The Treasure Coast Vintage Car Club's 45th annual Cars of Our Lives Show gives Sunday a change of pace, putting vintage, hot rod and custom automobiles in the spotlight in downtown Stuart. The event listing specifies that show vehicles must be at least 25 years old and asks owners to register early because space is limited.

 For spectators, it's a chance to explore a locally organized car show without an admission charge. Anyone planning to enter a vehicle should review the club's registration requirements rather than assume walk-up space is available. Car show details .

 Event times, admission prices and availability can change, especially over a busy holiday weekend. Check the linked organizers before leaving home. For more activities in all three counties, browse the Treasure Coast Today events calendar .

cards.headline: Martin County Commission Approves School Zone for Citrus Grove Elementary
cards.teaser: Martin County commissioners have unanimously approved a new school zone on Southwest Newfield Parkway outside Citrus Grove Elementary School, answering years of safety concerns fro
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners have unanimously approved a new school zone on Southwest Newfield Parkway outside Citrus Grove Elementary School, answering years of safety concerns from parents who say the current 45 mph speed limit puts children at risk. Many families who live in the Canopy Creek community across the street from the school walk their children to class each morning and afternoon, crossing the busy roadway.

 Kelly Ribaudo, the school's PTA president and Martin County PTA Advocacy Chair, said she has spent the last five years asking the county to install a school zone. "We've had so many near misses with the kids just from people not paying attention," Ribaudo said. "Everyone has a right to a free and public education and they should be safe getting there.

 "Our main priority should be the kids not the traffic." Parent Kendall George said the current traffic conditions frighten her. "It scares me," George said. "These cars are driving 45 miles an hour plus."

 At a previous Martin County Commission meeting, commissioners sided with the parents. "Whatever the number is there is no price to someone getting hurt," Commissioner Edward Ciampi said. "You will absolutely get a school zone." School Principal Rose Rynca said the need has grown as new communities bring more students to the area.

 "The amount of students crossing Newfield Parkway has definitely increased," Rynca said. "This speed zone is going to really really improve the safety of students." George said a school zone sign will help alert drivers. "It's letting drivers know that, hey there's a school here, there's children crossing, and we have to slow down," George said.

 A timeline for when the school zone will actually go in on Southwest Newfield Parkway has not been pinned down by the county. Until then, Ribaudo is urging drivers to use caution near the school regardless of posted signage. "Slow down if you see a school, even if there's not a school zone sign, slow down," Ribaudo said. With the school zone approved, parents say their next priority is pushing the county for better street lighting along the corridor.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Fire Board Fires Chief Jeff Lee, Names Langel Interim Chief
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Fire District Board voted Wednesday to fire Chief Jeff Lee without cause, capping months of controversy over a hazing investigation and a scathing no-confidenc
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District Board voted Wednesday to fire Chief Jeff Lee without cause, capping months of controversy over a hazing investigation and a scathing no-confidence vote from the firefighters' union. The board then voted 4-3 to appoint Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim chief while it searches for a permanent replacement.

 The meeting was packed with firefighters, union members, retirees and residents, many of whom urged commissioners to change the district's leadership. Taylor Baldwin pointed to dozens of supporters wearing yellow shirts throughout the room. "Look at everyone wearing yellow," Baldwin told commissioners.

 "These are not people who want to see the fire district fail. These are people who love this department enough to stand up and beg you to save it." A resident named Katie was more critical of the board itself. "You participated in this cover-up. You protected the lies and you profoundly failed the people you are elected to serve," she said.

 The controversy began this summer after a hazing investigation led the district to fire three veteran firefighters and suspend two others. The district determined the conduct amounted to hazing, while the firefighters and their union have argued it was consensual horseplay. A Fort Pierce Police Department investigation found no criminal violations, and the union is now pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated.

 The dispute escalated further when IAFF Local 1377 released results of a no-confidence vote earlier this month. According to the union, 423 of its 517 dues-paying members participated, and Lee received 314 no-confidence votes against 108 confidence votes, meaning 74.23% of participants said they no longer trusted his leadership.

 Lee joined the department in 1997 after serving in the U.S. Navy and became the district's 14th fire chief in May 2023. He was not present for Wednesday's meeting. Commissioners spent more than 30 minutes debating whether to fire him with or without cause before ultimately choosing to terminate him without cause, which triggers severance provisions in his contract.

 "I think we still have to come to the determination of what exactly the final total is of the severance," board member James Clasby said after the vote. "We will only pay what we are legally required to." Commissioner Jamie Fowler, who supported the removal, said the decision gives the district a chance at a fresh start. "I feel like a weight is lifted," Fowler said.

 "Firing someone is never an easy decision, regardless of all the factors that come into play. So I feel like we've sort of taken a step in the right direction." The board is moving forward with hiring outside legal counsel and discussing how it will select the district's next permanent chief. The board faced a similar decision in 2017, when it accepted then-Chief Buddy Emerson's immediate retirement after a prior union no-confidence vote and paid him severance through the end of his contract.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Council Gives Three Corners Developers Fourth Extension, Sets Dec. 8 Deadline
cards.teaser: The Vero Beach City Council has approved a fourth extension for ClearBlue, the developer negotiating the Three Corners project, giving the company until Dec. 8 to reach an agreemen
cards.body:
The Vero Beach City Council has approved a fourth extension for ClearBlue, the developer negotiating the Three Corners project, giving the company until Dec. 8 to reach an agreement on financing and lease terms or risk the city reconsidering the deal entirely.

 The Three Corners project is planned for the site of the old Vero Beach Power Plant at the base of the 17th Street Bridge, with proposals calling for hotels, a marina, restaurants and walking paths. Vero Beach Mayor John Cotugno said he has worked on the project since 2019 and wants the city to secure favorable terms for residents. "We need to negotiate the best, we'll call it a deal, for our citizens," Cotugno said.

 Cotugno said some progress has been made on the financial side of the developer's proposal, but he made clear that the council will walk away if ClearBlue's plans do not match the city's goals. "We need to listen and to see if this aligns with our goals and objectives. And if it does, great, we're going to work out a deal that's mutually beneficial," Cotugno said. "If not, then you know well we'll have to see what happens." To help close the gap, the council is appointing a liaison to work directly with the developers and bring them in for in-person discussions on the project.

 Bob Salera, a spokesperson for ClearBlue, said the company will meet with the city council on Oct. 27. He said ClearBlue had been requesting a liaison for months and welcomed the move. "It's something that we've actually been asking for for several months," Salera said.

 "We're glad we finally have one on the books now." Salera said ClearBlue has invested more than $1 million and 21,000 hours of work into the project and remains committed to finishing it. "We wouldn't have put in 21,000 hours of time into this project if we weren't serious," Salera said. "We're happy that these negotiations are moving forward, and we're ready to bring it home to a close." Cotugno said he shares that hope as long as both sides keep moving toward a resolution. "I'm willing to stay at that the table if progress is being made," he said.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Voters to Decide Sales Tax Renewal, Mosquito Control Expansion
cards.teaser: November's ballot asks St. Lucie County voters to renew a half-cent infrastructure sales tax for another decade and to expand mosquito control service into Tradition and the southwest county.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County voters will decide two ballot questions in November tied to the county's growing population and its strain on infrastructure and services. The first question asks voters to renew the existing half-cent sales tax, originally approved in 2018 and set to expire in two years, for another decade. The measure is not a new tax and would keep the total sales tax rate at 7%, with the half-cent portion continuing to fund infrastructure projects such as road improvements, sidewalks and stormwater drainage, along with larger projects like widening St. Lucie County roadways.

 "Now we're seeing that impact, you know, the delayed maintenance and the increased growth we've seen picked up, we're starting to have to play catch-up with those infrastructure projects and the needs are still there," said Erick Gill, communications director for St. Lucie County.

 The second ballot question asks voters whether to expand the county's mosquito control district to include the Tradition area and southwestern St. Lucie County, regions that have grown beyond the district's current service boundaries. Mosquito control services currently cover about half of the county's 600 square miles. If voters approve the expansion, affected property owners in those areas would pay about $28 more per year in taxes to fund fogging, spraying and mosquito surveillance.

 Both measures will appear on the November ballot and address separate needs as St. Lucie County continues to grow. County officials are encouraging voters to review their sample ballots ahead of time to see which questions apply to their specific address before heading to the polls.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Council Approves Lease for Marriott at Regional Airport
cards.teaser: Vero Beach City Council approved a lease agreement Tuesday to bring a four-story, 116-room Marriott hotel to the Vero Beach Regional Airport, ending three years of negotiations ove
cards.body:
Vero Beach City Council approved a lease agreement Tuesday to bring a four-story, 116-room Marriott hotel to the Vero Beach Regional Airport, ending three years of negotiations over the project. Developers said the hotel will break ground next year and is expected to be completed by the end of 2028.

 The hotel will sit just outside the gates of the airport terminal along Aviation Boulevard. Brian Dembeck, interim airport director, said the project will improve the experience for travelers passing through the airport. "We've been in negotiations with this for the last three years," Dembeck said. "This is something that is going to dramatically improve the passenger experience." Dembeck said passengers will be able to stay at the hotel while waiting for flights and walk straight over to the terminal.

 The hotel is intended to serve more than just airport passengers. Brian Cartland, vice-president of economic development for the Indian River County Chamber of Commerce, said the project could draw new business investment to the area. "The hotel is going to serve multiple purposes," Cartland said. "This hotel is going to help target industry growth by giving those companies that are looking at the area some additional alternatives for some great high-end options."

 Chad Maxey, senior vice president of Diversified Companies, the project's developer, said another major driver behind the hotel is its proximity to the Jackie Robinson Training Complex down the street. "We feel this is a great location to have a hotel that's going to be able to provide amenities to the airport and also to the families and kids that are going to play baseball," Maxey said.

 He said the hotel will include a "homerun dugout amenity" where families can enjoy virtual baseball. "Kids can play virtual baseball in the hotel as they're getting ready to go across the street and actually hit the diamond over there and play with the Major League Baseball players," Maxey said.

cards.headline: Martin County gives final approval to one-year data center moratorium in 4-0 vote
cards.teaser: Martin County commissioners gave final approval to a one-year pause on data center development after advancing it Oct. 13. A previously filed proposal off Kanner Highway remains exempt.
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners, who advanced a proposed one-year moratorium on new data center development Oct. 13, gave it final approval Tuesday, Oct. 27, in a unanimous 4-0 vote. The decision pauses new data center development while county leaders consider how to regulate the facilities, but a previously submitted proposal off Kanner Highway is exempt.

 The approval came at the moratorium’s second reading, following the earlier unanimous vote to move the measure forward. The one-year pause gives county officials time to consider how to handle future development of data centers. The Oct. 27 action completes the approval step that remained after commissioners advanced the proposal at their Oct. 13 meeting.

 The exempt application proposes a hyperscale data center off Kanner Highway west of Interstate 95. The county received it one day before commissioners first voted to advance the moratorium. Because the application was filed before the moratorium, the proposed project is not covered by the newly approved pause on development.

 The application was the county’s first-ever proposal for a data center in unincorporated Martin County. It arrived as residents raised concerns about the future of data center development and county leaders considered how the facilities should be regulated. The final vote establishes the one-year moratorium while leaving that previously filed application exempt from the restriction.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Approves Costco, Entertainment District, Rehab Hospital in Southern Grove
cards.teaser: The Port St. Lucie City Council has approved three major site plans for development in Southern Grove, the city's growing jobs corridor in western Port St. Lucie, including a long-
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council has approved three major site plans for development in Southern Grove, the city's growing jobs corridor in western Port St. Lucie, including a long-awaited Costco retail store. "This is something that we have been looking forward to for a long time," said Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie.

 The approved Costco store will total 163,000 square feet. Samples and Wes McCurry, president and CEO of the St. Lucie County Economic Development Council, said the store marks the beginning of a new phase of growth in the area. "This is getting closer to the finish line," Samples said.

 The Costco will join other companies already operating in Southern Grove, including Amazon, Tamco and Cheney Brothers. McCurry said the jobs already established in the corridor are now drawing new commercial development. "They see all the all the development that's occurring here, along with the demographics that they like to see," McCurry said. "It only makes sense that Costco opens a retail store here."

 The council also approved site plans for the first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District, a 5.5-acre project that will bring restaurants and retail to the area, along with plans for a new acute care rehabilitation hospital. "This area has historically been largely under-served by restaurants and retail, and especially entertainment facilities," McCurry said.

 "It's kind of catching up to the rooftops that are happening. You know, rooftops always drive that demand, but there's more to come." The rehabilitation hospital will offer inpatient and outpatient services with 42 beds in a building of more than 55,000 square feet. "Growing area needs services, and that's just another component of services that are coming into the area is expanded healthcare access," McCurry said.

 McCurry said the approvals reflect the realization of the city's long-term master plan for Southern Grove. "The plan is coming together. The vision is coming together.

 "What everyone saw 20 years ago is now starting to happen," he said. Samples said Costco still must close on the land and complete construction design planning and permitting before any construction begins.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested, accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger
hero.teaser: Investigators say Anthony Pizzarelli demanded an apology and support for government audits, including in St. Lucie County. He denied using his communications as leverage.
hero.body:
A Port St. Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he tried to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger by threatening lawsuits and ethics complaints unless she publicly apologized and supported government audits, including in St. Lucie County. The allegations against Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, are outlined in a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office probable cause affidavit.

 Pizzarelli faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. He told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he wanted an apology over an incident involving an email on which she had been copied and was seeking her support for his complaints. He is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

 Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9, offering to leave her out of planned lawsuits and ethics complaints if she issued a swift public apology. He proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, he wanted audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and investigations into government contracting.

 The affidavit says Pizzarelli sent a voice memo directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone on May 18, 2026. Among his statements were “I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice,” and “you don't know what I can do.” Weinberger told investigators she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family's safety. A first-term Republican, she represents Florida House District 94, which is entirely within Palm Beach County.

 In 2025, Pizzarelli was arrested after being accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies said the communications escalated in tone and content, raising concern among officials. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from that case had been dropped.

 Weinberger's campaign also faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election involving Nicholas Farley, not Pizzarelli. Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library.

cards.headline: 15-year-old and other driver seriously hurt in U.S. 1 crash near Treasure Coast Square Mall
cards.teaser: Stuart police say the fleeing driver in Tuesday’s wrong-way crash near Treasure Coast Square Mall was 15 years old. The teen and the other driver suffered serious injuries and were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center in Fort Pierce.
cards.body:
An Audi SUV traveling the wrong way during a police pursuit struck an oncoming vehicle Tuesday on U.S. 1 near Treasure Coast Square Mall, closing all southbound lanes. Stuart police now say the fleeing driver was 15 years old and that both drivers suffered serious injuries. Both were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center in Fort Pierce after the collision at the Mall South Entrance intersection.

 The pursuit began after officers conducting traffic enforcement near Southwest Federal Highway and Southwest St. Lucie Crescent spotted a vehicle traveling north at what they described as an extremely high rate of speed around 3:45 a.m. An officer attempted a traffic stop, but the driver refused to stop and fled, according to the Stuart Police Department.

 Police said the pursuit continued onto U.S. 1, where the fleeing driver began traveling north in the southbound lanes from Wright Boulevard. Officers continued trying to stop the vehicle because of the danger to other motorists and also tried to alert drivers traveling on Northwest Federal Highway, according to police.

 The fleeing vehicle then collided with a southbound vehicle at the mall entrance intersection. Officers learned after the crash that the fleeing driver was 15. Authorities previously said the pursuit involved Stuart Police and the Martin County Sheriff’s Office.

 The southbound lanes of U.S. 1 reopened around 7:58 a.m. The Stuart Police Department is investigating the incident, while the Florida Highway Patrol is conducting a separate investigation into the crash.

cards.headline: Arrest report details speeding, 0.246 blood-alcohol level in deputy's Vero Beach crash
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County sheriff’s deputy Tyler Horstman, arrested Monday on a felony DUI charge tied to a March 1 crash in Vero Beach, was driving 63 mph in a 35 mph zone and had a blood-
cards.body:
St. Lucie County sheriff’s deputy Tyler Horstman, arrested Monday on a felony DUI charge tied to a March 1 crash in Vero Beach, was driving 63 mph in a 35 mph zone and had a blood-alcohol level of 0.246, according to police and his arrest report. The woman driving the other vehicle suffered a traumatic brain injury, the report says. Horstman turned himself in Monday afternoon after a felony warrant was issued, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office.

 The crash happened about 11:25 p.m. at Beachland Boulevard and A1A. Horstman was off duty and driving an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office pickup truck when he struck a Chevy Equinox carrying the woman and an infant, according to the arrest report. Vero Beach police said Horstman entered the intersection on a green light and the other driver entered against a red light.

 Both drivers were injured and taken to the hospital. The infant was alert and responsive, according to the report.

 The arrest report says Horstman stated he had a few beers earlier in the evening. It describes a “faint odor of alcohol on his breath” and says he was “lethargic and dazed” and “drowsy and periodically dozing off.” The Sheriff’s Office received his blood-test results on September 9. His blood-alcohol concentration of 0.246 was more than three times Florida’s legal limit. Horstman was placed on administrative leave on September 15.

 The felony warrant issued Monday lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. Horstman was booked into the Indian River County Jail at 4:59 p.m. and posted $15,000 bond at 6:24 p.m. His arraignment is scheduled for December 9.

 Vero Beach police are leading the criminal investigation, according to the Sheriff’s Office. The agency’s internal investigation is on hold pending the outcome of the criminal case.

cards.headline: Man arrested after reported disturbance on Crooked Oak Avenue in Hobe Sound
cards.teaser: Joseph Oswald, 28, faces loitering, prowling and trespassing charges after residents called 911, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.
cards.body:
Joseph Oswald, 28, was arrested after residents along the 6000 block of Crooked Oak Avenue in Hobe Sound called 911 to report suspicious activity, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Deputies said he was yelling at people and wandering through the neighborhood.

 Responding deputies found Oswald appearing to be under the influence of an unknown substance, the sheriff's office said. He faces charges of loitering, prowling and trespassing.

 Oswald had been released from prison 11 days earlier. According to the sheriff's office, he has had as many as 14 prior arrests in Martin County on charges ranging from grand theft and burglary to loitering and prowling. The sheriff's office praised residents for quickly reporting the activity, saying community members play an important role in keeping their neighborhoods safe by reporting suspicious behavior.

cards.headline: Coastal flood warning covers St. Lucie County through 2 a.m. Thursday
cards.teaser: A coastal flood warning remains in effect for coastal St. Lucie County until 2 a.m. Thursday as king tides are expected to produce the season’s highest tides along Florida’s Atlant
cards.body:
A coastal flood warning remains in effect for coastal St. Lucie County until 2 a.m. Thursday, October 29, as king tides and rough surf raise the risk of significant flooding along Florida’s Atlantic coast. The National Weather Service warns that high water could inundate low-lying roads and waterfront properties around high tide, especially where drainage is poor. Residents should avoid flooded roads and follow local safety advisories.

 Thursday. The warning for coastal Palm Beach County lasts until 8 p.m. Wednesday. Monday’s highest tide is expected at 9:06 p.m.

 In Palm City, flooding has made SW Dyer Point Road impassable, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reported. Flooding was also reported on SW 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. Images released by the Sheriff’s Office show widespread water across streets, with people walking through water reaching their ankles.

 The agency is sending high-water rescue vehicles to assist people stranded in homes or vehicles. Residents should stay away from the flooded area and call 911 if they need emergency help. Drivers should never attempt to cross a flooded road and should turn around instead. A separate video shows flooding on Indian River Drive, with a car traveling through the water.

 In Boynton Beach, heavy flooding has closed the intersection of Ocean Avenue and Federal Highway. Drivers are being asked to stay clear of the intersection and take other routes. Officials plan to provide an update after the water drops and the intersection reopens.

 High tides have also forced the closure of Ocean Inlet Marina. Midtown Beach is temporarily closed because large surf and unusually high tides have made beach access unsafe, officials said. On South Ocean Boulevard, the northbound lane between Chilean Avenue and Australian Avenue will close from 10 a.m. to noon so crews can move a lifeguard tower.

 Other coastal recreation areas are also affected. Delray Beach officials say red flags are flying at the city’s beach because of high surf and flooding. The Juno Beach Pier is closed until further notice after sustaining damage from a recent offshore surge and high surf.

 Those closures accompany the coastal flood warnings covering Palm Beach, Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. With flooding more likely near high tide, residents in low-lying waterfront areas and places with poor drainage should avoid flooded roads. The safety message for motorists is to turn back rather than drive into floodwater.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Police: Missing 5-Year-Old Found Dead in Pond Near Portofino Landing
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police say a 5-year-old nonverbal girl who went missing from her apartment complex Saturday was found dead hours later in a nearby pond, with investigators now revealin
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police say a 5-year-old nonverbal girl who went missing from her apartment complex Saturday was found dead hours later in a nearby pond, with investigators now revealing new details about the search effort, including an attempt to track her location through a tablet she had with her. Mayra Glory Odelus was last seen before noon in the 5100 block of Portofino Landing Apartments east of Interstate 95.

 Her body was discovered in the pond at about 3 p.m., roughly 75 yards from her apartment, about three hours after she was reported missing. Police received the initial report at 11:39 a.m., and family members told officers Mayra was autistic and nonverbal.

 She was last seen wearing a dark oversized shirt with two white beads in her hair. Officers searched the surrounding area, handed out flyers with her name and photo, and flew drones over the area. Police called in Port St. Lucie bloodhounds and the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office dive team, which conducted an underwater search that led to the discovery of her body.

 According to police spokesperson Michael Santiago, Mayra had a tablet with her when she disappeared, and her family tried to locate her by pinging the device. The ping led searchers to the pond area, but at that point there was no sign of her, and the tablet itself has still not been recovered.

 Mayra's father told police the pond sits directly across from their apartment and that she loved the water. He and Mayra's 18-year-old sister were home at the time she went missing. Her mother lives in Haiti and was expected to arrive Sunday.

 "Our deepest condolences are with Mayra's family and loved ones during this tragic time," the Fort Pierce Police Department said in a statement. Santiago added, "It's very tragic when anything like this happens, but with our kids we have to make sure we're paying attention all the time, especially when kids are challenged with autism."

 Drowning remains the leading cause of unintentional death among children ages 1 to 3. Dr. Elizabeth Feldman of Cleveland Clinic Florida has said drowning can happen within seconds, and a lack of oxygen for just a few minutes can cause brain injury. The Children's Services Council of Palm Beach reported that 39 children with autism or suspected autism drowned in Florida in 2025, the highest number ever recorded in the state. The case has renewed attention on tracking and safety devices designed to prevent or respond to water-related emergencies involving children with autism, many of whom are drawn to water and may wander from supervision without being able to call for help.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Council Gives Three Corners Developers Fourth Extension, Sets Dec. 8 Deadline
cards.teaser: The Vero Beach City Council has approved a fourth extension for ClearBlue, the developer negotiating the Three Corners project, giving the company until Dec. 8 to reach an agreemen
cards.body:
The Vero Beach City Council has approved a fourth extension for ClearBlue, the developer negotiating the Three Corners project, giving the company until Dec. 8 to reach an agreement on financing and lease terms or risk the city reconsidering the deal entirely.

 The Three Corners project is planned for the site of the old Vero Beach Power Plant at the base of the 17th Street Bridge, with proposals calling for hotels, a marina, restaurants and walking paths. Vero Beach Mayor John Cotugno said he has worked on the project since 2019 and wants the city to secure favorable terms for residents. "We need to negotiate the best, we'll call it a deal, for our citizens," Cotugno said.

 Cotugno said some progress has been made on the financial side of the developer's proposal, but he made clear that the council will walk away if ClearBlue's plans do not match the city's goals. "We need to listen and to see if this aligns with our goals and objectives. And if it does, great, we're going to work out a deal that's mutually beneficial," Cotugno said. "If not, then you know well we'll have to see what happens." To help close the gap, the council is appointing a liaison to work directly with the developers and bring them in for in-person discussions on the project.

 Bob Salera, a spokesperson for ClearBlue, said the company will meet with the city council on Oct. 27. He said ClearBlue had been requesting a liaison for months and welcomed the move. "It's something that we've actually been asking for for several months," Salera said.

 "We're glad we finally have one on the books now." Salera said ClearBlue has invested more than $1 million and 21,000 hours of work into the project and remains committed to finishing it. "We wouldn't have put in 21,000 hours of time into this project if we weren't serious," Salera said. "We're happy that these negotiations are moving forward, and we're ready to bring it home to a close." Cotugno said he shares that hope as long as both sides keep moving toward a resolution. "I'm willing to stay at that the table if progress is being made," he said.

cards.headline: Martin County gives final approval to one-year data center moratorium in 4-0 vote
cards.teaser: Martin County commissioners gave final approval to a one-year pause on data center development after advancing it Oct. 13. A previously filed proposal off Kanner Highway remains exempt.
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners, who advanced a proposed one-year moratorium on new data center development Oct. 13, gave it final approval Tuesday, Oct. 27, in a unanimous 4-0 vote. The decision pauses new data center development while county leaders consider how to regulate the facilities, but a previously submitted proposal off Kanner Highway is exempt.

 The approval came at the moratorium’s second reading, following the earlier unanimous vote to move the measure forward. The one-year pause gives county officials time to consider how to handle future development of data centers. The Oct. 27 action completes the approval step that remained after commissioners advanced the proposal at their Oct. 13 meeting.

 The exempt application proposes a hyperscale data center off Kanner Highway west of Interstate 95. The county received it one day before commissioners first voted to advance the moratorium. Because the application was filed before the moratorium, the proposed project is not covered by the newly approved pause on development.

 The application was the county’s first-ever proposal for a data center in unincorporated Martin County. It arrived as residents raised concerns about the future of data center development and county leaders considered how the facilities should be regulated. The final vote establishes the one-year moratorium while leaving that previously filed application exempt from the restriction.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Approves Costco, Entertainment District, Rehab Hospital in Southern Grove
cards.teaser: The Port St. Lucie City Council has approved three major site plans for development in Southern Grove, the city's growing jobs corridor in western Port St. Lucie, including a long-
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council has approved three major site plans for development in Southern Grove, the city's growing jobs corridor in western Port St. Lucie, including a long-awaited Costco retail store. "This is something that we have been looking forward to for a long time," said Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie.

 The approved Costco store will total 163,000 square feet. Samples and Wes McCurry, president and CEO of the St. Lucie County Economic Development Council, said the store marks the beginning of a new phase of growth in the area. "This is getting closer to the finish line," Samples said.

 The Costco will join other companies already operating in Southern Grove, including Amazon, Tamco and Cheney Brothers. McCurry said the jobs already established in the corridor are now drawing new commercial development. "They see all the all the development that's occurring here, along with the demographics that they like to see," McCurry said. "It only makes sense that Costco opens a retail store here."

 The council also approved site plans for the first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District, a 5.5-acre project that will bring restaurants and retail to the area, along with plans for a new acute care rehabilitation hospital. "This area has historically been largely under-served by restaurants and retail, and especially entertainment facilities," McCurry said.

 "It's kind of catching up to the rooftops that are happening. You know, rooftops always drive that demand, but there's more to come." The rehabilitation hospital will offer inpatient and outpatient services with 42 beds in a building of more than 55,000 square feet. "Growing area needs services, and that's just another component of services that are coming into the area is expanded healthcare access," McCurry said.

 McCurry said the approvals reflect the realization of the city's long-term master plan for Southern Grove. "The plan is coming together. The vision is coming together.

 "What everyone saw 20 years ago is now starting to happen," he said. Samples said Costco still must close on the land and complete construction design planning and permitting before any construction begins.

cards.headline: Three generations later, Packard Roofing remains rooted on the Treasure Coast
cards.teaser: Founded in Miami in 1971 and established on the Treasure Coast in 1994, Packard Roofing & Waterproofing is now led by third-generation siblings Brian Packard and Stephanie Packard Smith.
cards.body:
For the Packard family, roofing has never been simply a business passed from one generation to the next. It has been a trade learned firsthand, a family responsibility and, over time, a connection to the communities the company serves.

 Packard Roofing & Waterproofing has grown from a South Florida roofing company into a multigenerational operation serving homeowners across Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties.

 The Port St. Lucie family business was founded in Miami in 1971 by Raymond M. Packard and David R. Packard. More than two decades later, the company expanded to Port St. Lucie in 1994, establishing the Treasure Coast operation that now serves customers across Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties.

 Today, the company is led by third-generation siblings Brian Packard and Stephanie Packard Smith.

 Brian's path into the family business started well before he was old enough to run one. As a teenager, he spent summers cleaning and organizing the warehouse and service yard. Later came tear-off crews, repair work, and eventually handling residential and commercial projects himself.

 Stephanie's history with the company also stretches back decades. She joined during the hectic aftermath of Hurricane Andrew in 1992, when South Florida roofing companies were dealing with enormous demand while Packard Roofing was also recovering from storm damage to its own facilities. She went on to become a central part of the company's office operations.

 Brian relocated from Miami to Port St. Lucie in 2021 as the family prepared for another transition. Following their father David Packard's death in 2022, Brian and Stephanie took responsibility for leading the company into its third generation.

 A business built around the Treasure Coast

 Packard Roofing's headquarters at 2182 NW Reserve Park Trace places the company beside PGA Village in Port St. Lucie, with much of its work concentrated throughout the Treasure Coast.

 The company handles roof repairs, roof replacements, new roof construction, and maintenance for homeowners throughout Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties.

 That local focus matters in a region where roofs face intense sun, heavy rainfall, tropical weather, and wind-driven rain. For homeowners, problems can range from persistent leaks and storm damage to aging roofs that have reached the end of their useful lifespan.

 Packard Roofing's website also provides homeowners with information about issues such as hurricane preparation, wind damage, roof leaks, and deciding when a roof should be repaired rather than replaced.

 For a company with decades behind it, that focus reflects an effort to remain useful to homeowners before they ever need a major roofing project.

 Experience that stayed with the company

 The Packard family is not the only long-term presence in the business.

 Superintendent Mark Hanna has worked with the company for more than 30 years, beginning as a repairman before moving into a leadership role overseeing repair and replacement work. His responsibilities now include supervising projects, preparing estimates, and often serving as one of the first people customers meet when they contact the company.

 That kind of employee longevity fits the broader story of a company that has transitioned across three generations without abandoning its family-business identity.

 Packard's philosophy, according to the family, has remained centered on straightforward communication, quality materials, and workmanship the company is willing to stand behind. The company says many customers return when they move to another home or recommend Packard to younger generations of their own families.

 Looking toward another generation

 More than five decades after the company was founded, Packard Roofing is operating in a Treasure Coast that looks very different from the one it entered in the 1990s.

 Port St. Lucie has grown around it. PGA Village and surrounding communities have expanded. New homes continue to rise while existing roofs move through the repair and replacement cycle that comes with age and Florida weather.

 The business has changed with that growth, but its leadership still describes Packard in distinctly family terms.

 For Brian, continuing the company means carrying forward standards established by his grandfather and father rather than simply preserving a business name. He has described honesty, hard work and quality craftsmanship as values passed down through three generations.

 Packard Roofing & Waterproofing provides roof repair, replacement, maintenance, and new-roof construction throughout Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties.

 Packard Roofing & Waterproofing 

 2182 NW Reserve Park Trace, Port St. Lucie, FL

 772-468-3723

 PackardRoofing.com

cards.headline: New Ikonick Energetics Primer Plant in Indiantown Adds 100-Plus Jobs to Martin County
cards.teaser: Ikonick Energetics has opened a new primer manufacturing facility in Indiantown, expanding its ammunition production operation in Martin County and adding more than 100 jobs across
cards.body:
Ikonick Energetics has opened a new primer manufacturing facility in Indiantown, expanding its ammunition production operation in Martin County and adding more than 100 jobs across its two local sites. The expansion comes as Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties continue to report unemployment rates above the statewide average.

 The Indiantown facility makes primers, one of four components used to build ammunition. Richard Rhatigan, vice president of law enforcement and government sales at Ikonick USA, said the plant has significant production capacity. "At full capacity you're looking at a billion primers per year," Rhatigan said. He explained the role primers play in the finished product: "It is one of the four components that go into building ammunition, so the primer actually ignites the powder which is incased within the brass."

 Cameras were not permitted inside the Indiantown primer facility, but Ikonick gave a look at its ammunition manufacturing operation in Stuart, where workers combine the primer, brass casing and projectile to produce finished rounds. With the addition of the Indiantown plant, the company says about 75% of each piece of ammunition is now produced in Martin County.

 The new hires are expected to include both entry-level and specialized manufacturing positions. "When you talk about American manufacturing what that really means is, the people who work in our facilities, they live in our community," Rhatigan said.

 Rhatigan said the company sees room for more growth in the area. "The opportunity for expansion is here and it is part of supporting the community in Martin County," he said. The Indiantown Chamber of Commerce said the new facility represents a significant investment in advanced manufacturing for the region.

 Ikonick also said its Martin County operations will help meet ammunition needs for law enforcement training. "We can support the state and local law enforcement training needs with our ammo with our facility in Stuart and here in Indiantown," Rhatigan said. For Indiantown, the facility adds to the community's manufacturing sector and could bring further employment opportunities as Ikonick continues to expand.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Residents Escalate to EPA Over ALF Project Near Contaminated Site
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie's City Council already approved the major site plan for a 150-unit assisted-living facility next to a petroleum-contaminated property, but residents say an engineering letter shows cleanup plans had to be revised because of the project. Neighbors have now contacted the EPA and Florida Department of Health seeking answers.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie's City Council has approved the major site plan for a 150-unit assisted-living facility planned next to a petroleum-contaminated property, a decision residents are now pushing back on by contacting federal and state environmental agencies. The project, known as PSL Westmoreland ALF, is planned for 7.1 acres within the Rivella planned unit development along Southeast Morningside Boulevard near Southeast Westmoreland Boulevard.

 The three-story facility would include assisted-living units and a memory care component. Residents say they have reached out to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Florida Department of Health seeking more information about the neighboring property's contamination history.

 An engineering letter obtained by residents adds new detail to their concerns. The letter, from BTEX Engineering, discusses a March 2026 meeting with environmental officials about the neighboring contaminated property and states that the proposed remediation approach should be changed because of concerns about surrounding properties, including the planned assisted-living facility. The letter also says vapors would need to be captured during the remediation process.

 Resident David Lipps said the issue is not about what is being built on the site, arguing that nearby businesses and other facilities could also be affected by environmental concerns tied to the contaminated property. Resident Charlie D'Agata said residents have raised objections at City Council meetings for about two years and questioned why a developer would be allowed to build near a property he described as contaminated.

 Construction on the assisted-living facility has not begun. Although the City Council approved the project's major site plan in September, the developer must still submit construction plans for technical review, followed by additional reviews involving the South Florida Water Management District and other agencies. The environmental history of the neighboring property and the extent of any potential impact on surrounding land remain central questions for residents, who say they want clearer answers about how any risks would be addressed as the project moves forward.

hero.headline: Jensen Beach captures District 13-4A football title against Fort Pierce Westwood
hero.teaser: Jensen Beach faced Fort Pierce Westwood on Friday with the District 13-4A football championship at stake, seeking its fourth district title in five years. The Falcons entered the m
hero.body:
Jensen Beach faced Fort Pierce Westwood on Friday with the District 13-4A football championship at stake, seeking its fourth district title in five years. The Falcons entered the matchup after a 51-0 victory over Legacy the previous week, a shutout highlighted by two defensive touchdowns from senior linebacker Alex Thornton. The district contest put Jensen Beach among the Treasure Coast teams playing for championship honors on a night that also brought a title-winning performance from Vero Beach. For the Falcons, the matchup with Westwood offered an opportunity to add another championship to their recent run of district success.

 Thornton supplied two of the biggest plays in Jensen Beach’s win over Legacy, returning a pair of interceptions for touchdowns. His scoring returns were part of a performance in which the Falcons held their opponent scoreless while putting up 51 points. That result gave Jensen Beach momentum heading into its meeting with Fort Pierce Westwood, where the stakes shifted to the district championship. The Falcons’ pursuit of a fourth title in five years was a central storyline entering Friday’s game, following a week in which their defense contributed both points and a shutout.

 Vero Beach secured the District 8-6A championship by defeating rival Treasure Coast 24-0 on Friday. The Fighting Indians’ defense kept Treasure Coast off the scoreboard, continuing its strong play late in the season. The victory stretched Vero Beach’s winning streak to six games and added a district championship to that run.

 Vero Beach had been pursuing a third straight district title, and the shutout against its rival continued the program’s sustained success in district competition. While Jensen Beach entered its matchup seeking another championship, Vero Beach delivered a title-clinching result with a three-touchdown margin and a clean defensive performance against Treasure Coast.

 Elsewhere in the region, lightning affected the Friday schedule in Palm Beach County. Delays pushed back the start of play, but Dwyer and Royal Palm Beach eventually got underway. Benjamin was also in action at home, where its promising young players were among the featured performers.

 Those games formed part of a regional football night that included championship stakes, a rivalry shutout and weather interruptions. On the Treasure Coast, the district picture was the main focus: Vero Beach celebrated its District 8-6A title, while Jensen Beach’s meeting with Fort Pierce Westwood carried the District 13-4A championship stakes.

cards.headline: Jensen Beach's Andrew Burnette wins legal fight for fifth year, returns to Louisiana Tech
cards.teaser: Jensen Beach native Andrew Burnette has won back a fifth season of college football eligibility after taking his case to court against the NCAA, and he is now back on the field at
cards.body:
Jensen Beach native Andrew Burnette has won back a fifth season of college football eligibility after taking his case to court against the NCAA, and he is now back on the field at Louisiana Tech. Burnette moved to Martin County from Michigan around age 12 and went on to star at Jensen Beach High School, where he originally enrolled to wrestle before football took over as his main focus.

 "I wasn't zoned for that school, but I went there for wrestling originally; that was my first passion," Burnette said. "Moving through high school, I knew football was what I wanted to do."

 Despite his success at Jensen Beach High School, Burnette said he did not draw much interest from college recruiters, a common experience for Treasure Coast football players. "One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited," he said. He chose to play at Highland Community College in Kansas, where he rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns in nine games, but still failed to attract bigger programs. He then transferred to Independence Junior College, a school featured on the Netflix series Last Chance U, but was cut from that team.

 Burnette reached out to Keiser University in West Palm Beach, reminding the coaching staff that they had offered him a spot back in high school. "I spoke with the coach there and told him, 'You guys offered me in high school,' and he said, 'I don't really remember. Send me your film.' He saw my film and said, 'Hey, bring it,'" Burnette said.

 Over two seasons at Keiser, he rushed for more than 2,300 yards and scored 30 touchdowns, numbers that finally caught the attention of Division I programs, including Louisiana Tech. He played his first Division I season there last year, but his NCAA eligibility ran out under the old four-year limit.

 Rather than walk away from the game, Burnette called his father and took a job working alongside him at a steel mill in Detroit. "I called my dad and told him, 'Hey, I need to do something. I can't just sit here,' so I went and worked with my dad in Michigan," he said.

 This summer the NCAA adopted a new 5-in-5 rule, allowing athletes to compete in up to five seasons within a continuous five-year window. Burnette hired a lawyer and took his case to court against the NCAA, which granted him a final season of eligibility. He is now back on the field at Louisiana Tech. "It was amazing; I would rather play football than do anything, and for me to have this opportunity again, it's a blessing," Burnette said.

cards.headline: Stuart's Atlantic Diving Team trains young divers toward scholarships and Olympic goals
cards.teaser: Young divers with Stuart's Atlantic Diving Team are training under coach Pito Alberty with hopes of college scholarships, international competition and the Olympics.
cards.body:
A group of young divers in Stuart is training with hopes that their sport will carry them to college scholarships, international competition and even the Olympics. The athletes train with the Atlantic Diving Team under coach Osvaldo "Pito" Alberty, who teaches divers of all ages, backgrounds and experience levels the Olympic sport of diving.

 Grace Erickson, a local diver now in eighth grade, said diving has been her passion since early childhood. "On my preschool poster I wrote what I wanted to be when I got older was a diver," Erickson said. She said the sport keeps surprising her.

 "It's been really exciting; it's new things every twist and turn, both in your head and diving off the board," Erickson said. Erickson said she has come to love platform diving in particular, along with the friendships she has built with teammates over the years. She hopes to take her diving to the college level.

 Alberty, who has coached Erickson for years, said he wants to see her and her teammates push the sport to new heights. "We are like a family here. We treat each other with respect and courtesy, and we push each other to do better than everyone else," Alberty said.

 He said starting divers young opens doors down the road. "The younger we get them, the better it is because over time they can get scholarships. If they want to do international diving, they can qualify for international competitions or even the Olympics," Alberty said.

 Among the team's newer members is 14-year-old Carissa Smith, who switched from gymnastics to diving about two months ago. Smith said her gymnastics background has helped her adjust to the new sport, though she has not yet competed because she wants to master the basics first. "I was recently a gymnast and just about two months ago I started diving," Smith said.

 She said the sport has already won her over. "It feels like you're flying; it's exhilarating just being able to get better at my diving," Smith said.

cards.headline: P1 Motor Club's First Racetrack 85% Done on Former St. Lucie Orange Grove
cards.teaser: Members are expected to hit the first track within a month at the 650-acre P1 Motor Club on Okeechobee Road, where entry starts at $192,000 and 68 real estate units have already sold.
cards.body:
P1 Motor Club expects to welcome members onto its first racetrack within a month at its 650-acre development on Okeechobee Road in St. Lucie County. The property, taking shape on a former orange grove, is planned around nearly 10 miles of driving surfaces, trackside homes and country club style amenities. Membership currently starts at $192,000, with yearly dues on top of that cost.

 Chris Duplessis, P1's director of fun, said the club's three-mile track is about 85% complete, with remaining work limited to finishing guardrail sections while newly laid asphalt cures. Construction on the track visible today started about a year ago, following several years of planning and approvals. Duplessis compared the concept to a high-end golf club, but with race cars instead of golf balls. The club plans to pay for a water line connecting the development to county water service.

 Duplessis said P1 already has 280 members and has sold 68 real estate units. Planned garage townhomes will place vehicle space on the ground floor with living areas upstairs, and every unit is designed to overlook the track. P1 also plans trackside residences, and Duplessis estimated the development will eventually include roughly 200 residential units, many expected to serve as second or third homes.

 Only members can buy real estate, with homes quoted at $1.4 million purchased separately from membership. Duplessis said residents could begin moving in within about two years, with the full development expected to take approximately five years to complete.

 Construction on the larger 4.5-mile circuit and the real estate portion is expected to begin around the start of 2027. That circuit will include elevation changes and a crossover bridge where the track passes over itself, along with planned karting, rally and drifting areas. P1's partnership with Mercedes will supply a fleet of vehicles for members without their own cars, and Duplessis described plans for Mercedes-hosted driving experiences open to nonmembers.

 Beginners will get instructors to teach driving fundamentals and track rules before advancing, and members whose skills qualify can join club races. The development's broader plans include a clubhouse with a rooftop bar, a pool, pickleball and other sport courts, lakes, walking trails and a motorsports business park. Duplessis, a four-time national rally champion, said he plans to live on the property himself. He said P1 will use local contractors and workers and expects a busy day to draw about 100 members.

cards.headline: 17 businesses raise over $10,000 for Sebastian River High play clocks after coach's Facebook post
cards.teaser: Seventeen local businesses raised more than $10,000 for new play clocks at Sebastian River High School after coach Phinehas Weatherly posted about equipment problems on Facebook.
cards.body:
Seventeen local businesses raised more than $10,000 for new play clocks at Sebastian River High School after coach Phinehas Weatherly posted about equipment problems on Facebook.

 Weatherly said the varsity football program has struggled with malfunctioning play clocks for four years. Each repair cost thousands of dollars.

 "For the last four years, it's been a battle of trying to get a working play clock, which is essential when you're trying to run an offense and keep it moving and not get delay games," Weatherly said.

 Weatherly made a Facebook post saying the situation was ridiculous and that the school could not get basic equipment while other schools received more support. Sebastian River alum Bryan Rhoades saw the post and shared his own video online asking the community to help.

 "I need five business owners or people, whoever, to match my $1,000. We can get this done," Rhoades said.

 Rhoades owns Airbnbs in the area and River Ride Cart Rentals LLC. The response was swift.

 "Within like an hour I had $2,000 and within I think three more days we had $10,350," Rhoades said.

 The old play clocks were stationary and had suffered significant wear and tear over the years, requiring repeated electrical repairs and parts replacements. The new clocks are lit up, bright and roll around so they can be kept out of the weather.

 "For the longest time, it seemed like we were just getting pushed to the side. And to see that there's people out there that still care and want to support and want to help, you know, it was great. It was amazing," Weatherly said.

 Rhoades said the support reflected the character of the Sebastian community.

 "They just want to get out there and help. That's what it comes down to really. You know what I mean, the kids," Rhoades said.

 The new play clocks are expected to debut at Sebastian River's next home football game in October.

cards.headline: Vero Beach gym owner helps Team USA win gold in paintball at France event
cards.teaser: Paige Vasser, owner of Legacy Boxing Gym in Vero Beach, helped Team USA win gold last weekend at an international paintball competition in France, capping a rapid rise that has pla
cards.body:
Paige Vasser, owner of Legacy Boxing Gym in Vero Beach, helped Team USA win gold last weekend at an international paintball competition in France, capping a rapid rise that has placed her among the top-10 professional women in the sport.

 Vasser grew up in Southeast Georgia near Brunswick before moving to Sebastian, where she eventually opened Legacy Boxing Gym in Vero Beach. She never played a sport until she was 21 years old. Her introduction to athletics came through boxing, which she embraced fully despite having never exercised before.

 Vasser said she thought boxing was, in her words, badass. Her boyfriend, who had been playing paintball for about 10 years, later introduced her to the sport. She took her team at Legacy for a day of paintballing and quickly fell in love with it as a weekend activity that kept them busy.

 What started as a weekend hobby quickly turned into something much bigger. A coach noticed Vasser playing and recruited her for his divisional team. A year later, she signed with her first women's professional team.

 Her rise through the sport has been rapid, placing her among the top professional women in paintball. Last weekend she competed internationally when she flew into Paris for an event in France.

 The event was held at the site of the United Paintball Federation, where Vasser and Team USA won gold in one of the largest competitions in the sport. Vasser said she got to play with girls she never played with before, calling it an awesome experience. She said the other players were amazing and it was a lot of fun.

 The gym owner's journey from someone who never played sports or exercised before age 21 to becoming an international gold medalist in paintball highlights her rapid development in the sport. Her story demonstrates how a weekend pastime can evolve into professional athletic success when combined with dedication and natural talent.

cards.headline: Vero Beach quarterback Champ Monds done for season after medical procedure
cards.teaser: Vero Beach High School star quarterback Champ Monds announced Saturday on Instagram that he has played his final game for the Fighting Indians after an unexpected medical procedure
cards.body:
Vero Beach High School star quarterback Champ Monds announced Saturday on Instagram that he has played his final game for the Fighting Indians after an unexpected medical procedure ended his senior season.

 Monds wrote that his 2026 season has been cut short due to an unexpected minor procedure that needs to be addressed. The four-star quarterback and Notre Dame commit is just 16 years old. He reclassified to the 2027 recruiting class after being rated as the top quarterback in the country for 2028.

 The Fighting Indians were in the midst of another strong season. Monds helped lead Vero Beach to an undefeated regular season last year, though he dealt with an injury during that campaign as well. The team lost in the 7A state championship game in the final seconds.

 Monds stands at 6-foot-3 and 230 pounds. The son of a pro baseball player and grandson of an NFL player, he made his college commitment live on the Pat McAfee show on ESPN. Monds chose Notre Dame over Ohio State and Florida State.

 He said Notre Dame head coach Marcus Freeman and the coaching staff made him feel at home during his spring visit. Monds said it was kind of an easy decision after the coaching staff and players treated him with the utmost respect during his spring practice visit. He will play for the Fighting Irish next season.

hero.headline: Looking for something to do Halloween weekend? Here are the Top 5 local events for Oct. 30-Nov. 1
hero.teaser: A free Port St. Lucie fall festival, Halloween fun with wildlife in Hobe Sound, live music in Fort Pierce and Vero Beach, and a classic car show in Stuart lead this weekend's picks.
hero.body:
Halloween falls on Saturday this year, and the Treasure Coast has plenty happening from Friday evening through Sunday. Families can kick off the weekend with carnival rides and trick-or-treating in Port St. Lucie or get a closer look at animal ambassadors in Hobe Sound. Saturday offers a Halloween-themed Blues Brothers tribute in Fort Pierce and an eclectic live-music set in Vero Beach, while Sunday brings a vintage car show to downtown Stuart.

 Here are five standout events for Friday evening, Oct. 30, Saturday, Oct. 31, and Sunday, Nov. 1 , across Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties.

 When: Friday, Oct. 30, 5-10 p.m. Where: MIDFLORIDA Event Center, 9221 SE Event Center Place, Port St. Lucie. Admission: Free; check with the organizer about individual attractions and purchases.

 The MIDFLORIDA Event Center's Fall Fun Fest opens the weekend with live music, carnival rides, food, family activities and trick-or-treating. The organizer describes it as a three-day event, making this a centerpiece of the Halloween weekend calendar.

 The confirmed Friday hours are 5-10 p.m.; check the event center's listing for the schedules on its other dates and any costs beyond general admission. Festival details .

 2. Creepy Creature Feature, Hobe Sound

 When: Friday, Oct. 30, 5:30-7:30 p.m. Where: Hobe Sound Nature Center, 13640 SE Federal Highway, Hobe Sound. Admission: Not specified in the calendar; confirm with the organizer.

 The Hobe Sound Nature Center brings back its family-friendly Creepy Creature Feature for a wildlife-themed Halloween evening. The event listing highlights glitter tattoos and the center's animal ambassadors among the attractions.

 It's a seasonal option for families who would rather spend part of Halloween weekend meeting animals than attending a conventional costume party. Check the organizer for participation details before going. Event details .

 3. Jake and Elwood Blues Revue and Halloween look-alike contest, Fort Pierce

 When: Saturday, Oct. 31, 1-4 p.m.; look-alike contest listed for 3 p.m. Where: Summer Crush Vineyard & Winery, 4200 Johnston Road, Fort Pierce. Admission: $18.50 listed in the TCT events calendar; confirm current ticket terms with the organizer.

 A six-piece Blues Brothers tribute act takes the stage at Summer Crush Vineyard & Winery for a Halloween afternoon of music. The listing also advertises a Jake-and-Elwood-style look-alike contest at 3 p.m., giving visitors a reason to work the duo's signature look into their costumes.

 For anyone seeking live entertainment rather than a traditional trick-or-treating outing, this combines a concert with a holiday costume competition. Show details .

 4. Hot Sauce Moon at Riverside Theatre, Vero Beach

 When: Saturday, Oct. 31, 5:30-8:30 p.m. Where: Riverside Theatre, 3250 Riverside Park Drive, Vero Beach. Admission: Not specified in the calendar; check the venue.

 Hot Sauce Moon provides an Indian River County option for Halloween night. Riverside Theatre describes the band's sound as an eclectic mix of classic rock, folk rock, country and blues, with the performance listed on its Loop Music Calendar.

 The evening set is an alternative for readers who want to hear live music after daytime Halloween activities. Verify seating and admission arrangements with Riverside Theatre. Music calendar .

 5. Cars of Our Lives Show, Stuart

 When: Sunday, Nov. 1, 9 a.m.-3 p.m. Where: City of Stuart Water Tower, 301 SE Stypmann Boulevard, Stuart. Admission: Free.

 The Treasure Coast Vintage Car Club's 45th annual Cars of Our Lives Show gives Sunday a change of pace, putting vintage, hot rod and custom automobiles in the spotlight in downtown Stuart. The event listing specifies that show vehicles must be at least 25 years old and asks owners to register early because space is limited.

 For spectators, it's a chance to explore a locally organized car show without an admission charge. Anyone planning to enter a vehicle should review the club's registration requirements rather than assume walk-up space is available. Car show details .

 Event times, admission prices and availability can change, especially over a busy holiday weekend. Check the linked organizers before leaving home. For more activities in all three counties, browse the Treasure Coast Today events calendar .

cards.headline: Veterans Day Golf Fundraiser Comes to Hobe Sound's Lost Lake Club
cards.teaser: Tee It Up for the Troops will bring its Veterans Day golf fundraiser to The Club at Lost Lake in Hobe Sound for the first time this year. The tournament is scheduled for Wednesday,
cards.body:
Tee It Up for the Troops will bring its Veterans Day golf fundraiser to The Club at Lost Lake in Hobe Sound for the first time this year. The tournament is scheduled for Wednesday, Nov. 11, at the club, located at 8300 SE Fazio Drive. The field is capped at 106 golfers, with registration priced at $750 per player, and local veterans paired into foursomes will play for free.

 Chris LaRocque, president and executive director of Tee It Up for the Troops, said the cause is personal. "It's very close to my heart," LaRocque said in an interview with ARC Florida. "I'm an Army Reserve major myself." LaRocque said the nonprofit has deployed more than $20 million and supported more than 400,000 veterans through programs that help with the transition to civilian jobs and provide support for post-traumatic stress disorder and traumatic brain injuries.

 Proceeds from the Hobe Sound tournament will also benefit local veterans programs, including PGA HOPE in South Florida, according to LaRocque. PGA HOPE introduces veterans and active-duty service members to golf as a way to support their physical, mental, social and emotional well-being.

 Registration and event information for the tournament are available through Tee It Up for the Troops.

cards.headline: Looking for something to do this weekend? Here are the Top 5 local events for Oct. 24-25
cards.teaser: A free science festival in Fort Pierce, trick-or-treating in Stuart, a Tradition fall market, Sunday jazz and a guided bat hike lead this weekend's Treasure Coast picks.
cards.body:
With Halloween just around the corner, this weekend's Treasure Coast calendar has plenty to offer beyond the usual routine. A major hands-on science festival heads to a new Fort Pierce venue, downtown Stuart welcomes families for an early round of trick-or-treating, and Tradition hosts an afternoon of fall festivities. Sunday's picks range from free jazz in the park to an evening search for bats along a preserve trail.

 Here are five standout events for Saturday, Oct. 24, and Sunday, Oct. 25 , across Martin and St. Lucie counties.

 1. Indian River Lagoon Science Festival, Fort Pierce

 When: Saturday, Oct. 24, 10 a.m.-3 p.m. Where: Museum Pointe Park, 414 Seaway Drive, Fort Pierce. Admission: Free.

 The 11th annual Indian River Lagoon Science Festival brings hands-on experiments, demonstrations and local science organizations together for a day of discovery. More than 50 exhibitors are expected, with activities covering science, technology, engineering, art and math. Organizers highlight marine mammal rescue, sea turtles, underwater robots and even a chance to learn how crime-scene investigators work.

 Important location change: This year's festival is at Museum Pointe Park, between the St. Lucie County Aquarium and the regional history center, rather than its previous location. Organizers also list free parking at Causeway Cove Marina, along with complimentary admission to the aquarium and history center during the festival. Festival details .

 2. Hobgoblins on Main Street, Stuart

 When: Saturday, Oct. 24, noon-3 p.m. Where: Riverwalk Stage and surrounding historic downtown Stuart. Admission: Free.

 Downtown Stuart is getting into the Halloween spirit with the 27th annual Hobgoblins on Main Street, presented by Stuart Main Street and the Historic Downtown Business Association. The afternoon is designed around family-friendly, safe trick-or-treating, giving children a chance to celebrate Halloween a week early.

 With the activity centered around downtown's Riverwalk Stage, this is an easy choice for families who want an afternoon outing without traveling far between stops. Event details .

 3. IL Merchato Fall-O-Ween Market, Port St. Lucie

 When: Saturday, Oct. 24, 1-7 p.m. Where: Tradition Square, SW Meeting Street, Port St. Lucie. Admission: Free general admission.

 Tradition Square will host a fall and Halloween-themed market with local vendors, food trucks and activities for children. Organizers list trick-or-treating, bounce houses, face painting, costumed character meet-and-greets and a seasonal photo booth among the attractions.

 The event offers a longer afternoon-to-evening window than many of Saturday's activities, making it another option for families planning around the day's other commitments. Costumes are encouraged. Event details .

 4. Sunday Jazz in the Park, Stuart

 When: Sunday, Oct. 25, 3-6 p.m. Where: Memorial Park, 300 SE Ocean Blvd., Stuart. Admission: Free.

 The nonprofit Music4Unity is kicking off its fifth season of Sunday Jazz in the Park with an afternoon of contemporary jazz and classic R&B. DJ Celo is scheduled to start the music at 3 p.m., followed by a live performance from the Charles Jones Trio at 5 p.m.

 Visitors are encouraged to bring lawn chairs, blankets and coolers to settle in under the park's banyan trees. For anyone looking for a relaxed Sunday afternoon rather than another Halloween event, this is one of the weekend's strongest options. Concert details .

 5. Going Batty Full Moon Hike, Port St. Lucie

 When: Sunday, Oct. 25, 6:30-8 p.m. Where: Spruce Bluff Preserve, 611 Dar Lane, Port St. Lucie. Admission: Check the organizer for registration and participation details.

 Sunday evening offers a different kind of seasonal adventure: a guided nature outing in search of Florida's bats. Participants will look for bats flying, roosting or making calls along the trail while learning about their place in the local ecosystem.

 The program is described as appropriate for ages 8 and older . It is a fitting way to close a Halloween-season weekend, particularly for families interested in wildlife rather than costumes and candy. Review participation requirements before heading to the preserve. Hike details .

 Schedules and participation details can change, so check with organizers before leaving home. For more activities throughout Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties, browse the Treasure Coast Today events calendar .
