The Treasure Coast's first big October weekend brings two days of fall festivals, an outdoor craft fair, a community-wide preview in Port St. Lucie and an early Halloween outing for families. Here are five events worth considering for Saturday, Oct. 10, and Sunday, Oct. 11.

 1. Newfield Harvest Festival, Palm City

 When: Saturday and Sunday, Oct. 10-11, noon to 6 p.m. each day. Where: Newfield Fields, Palm City. Admission: Free.

 Newfield's first annual Harvest Festival offers a full weekend of fall activities, with a Ferris wheel, pumpkin picking, a hay maze and hayrides among the attractions listed by organizers. Live music, local vendors and family activities round out the two-day celebration.

 The festival is a strong choice for families looking to spend an afternoon outdoors rather than squeeze multiple stops into a single outing. Event details .

 2. Downtown Stuart Fall Craft Festival, Stuart

 When: Saturday and Sunday, Oct. 10-11, starting at 10 a.m. each day; scheduled through 5 p.m. Sunday. Where: Osceola Street, downtown Stuart. Admission: Free.

 The 27th annual Downtown Stuart Fall Craft Festival brings an outdoor art and craft show to Osceola Street in the historic waterfront district. Visitors can browse the displays and explore nearby downtown shops and restaurants during the festival weekend.

 The event offers an easy way to make a day of downtown Stuart, whether the main draw is handmade goods or a walk around the waterfront area. Event details .

 3. Tradition Unlocked, Port St. Lucie

 When: Saturday and Sunday, Oct. 10-11; activities are scheduled across the weekend, with individual stop times varying. Where: Multiple locations in Tradition, Port St. Lucie. Admission: Free.

 Tradition Unlocked invites households to explore several venues for a preview of activities and events planned for next year. Each stop reveals something different, and visitors can complete a Tradition Passport by visiting the participating locations for a chance to enter a drawing.

 Because the program spans several stops, check the daily itinerary before heading out. Saturday details and Sunday details .

 4. Trick or Treat Stroll, Jensen Beach

 When: Saturday, Oct. 10, 4-6 p.m.; members may enter at 3:30 p.m. Where: Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast, Jensen Beach. Admission: $3 per person ages 1 and older, including members and nonmembers.

 The Children's Museum gets an early start on Halloween with its Trick or Treat Stroll. The Saturday afternoon event offers families a seasonal outing well ahead of Oct. 31, with the museum setting the price at $3 for children and adults ages 1 and up.

 Families planning to attend should review the organizer's event information for any participation details before leaving home. Event details .

 5. Tribute to Chicago and Other Great Horn Bands, Fort Pierce

 When: Sunday, Oct. 11, 1-4 p.m. Where: Summer Crush Vineyard & Winery, Fort Pierce. Admission: Listed at $18.50.

The performance adds a live-music option to a weekend otherwise heavy on fall festivals and family activities.

 Check current admission and availability with the venue before making plans. Event details .

cards.headline: Looking for something to do this weekend? Here are the Top 5 local events for Oct. 3-4
cards.teaser: From a free Bahamian festival in Stuart and a two-day makers market in Port St. Lucie to Oktoberfest, live music in Vero Beach and a Sunday car show in Fort Pierce, here are five Treasure Coast events worth checking out this weekend.
cards.body:
The first weekend of October brings a mix of cultural celebrations, outdoor markets, live music and seasonal events across the Treasure Coast.

 Treasure Coast Today reviewed this weekend's local event listings and picked five that stand out for their mix of broad appeal, local character and variety across Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties.

 1. 30th Annual Bahamian Festival — Stuart

 The 30th Annual Bahamian Festival takes over New Monrovia Park in Stuart on Saturday with a full day centered on Bahamian culture.

 The free community celebration runs from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. and is set to include Bahamian food vendors and live island music. The long Saturday schedule makes this one of the weekend's biggest all-day community events.

 When: Saturday, Oct. 3, 11 a.m.–7 p.m. Where: New Monrovia Park, 4453 SE Murray St., Stuart Cost: Free Details: View the TCT event listing 2. Florida Creatives Market — Port St. Lucie

 If you want an event that works on either Saturday or Sunday, the Florida Creatives Market is the easiest pick on this list.

 The free, two-day outdoor market at Clover Park is bringing together local makers, artists, small businesses and food vendors, with beverages and music also part of the event. It runs Saturday and Sunday, giving shoppers a full weekend to stop by.

 When: Saturday, Oct. 3 through Sunday, Oct. 4 Where: Clover Park, 31 Piazza Drive, Port St. Lucie Cost: Free Details: View the TCT event listing 3. Oktoberfest — Port St. Lucie

 Saturday evening brings Oktoberfest to the MIDFLORIDA Event Center, with an event lineup built around German music, dancing, Bavarian food and one particularly hard-to-ignore attraction: a wiener dog race.

 The event runs from 5 to 9 p.m., making it a good evening option after one of the daytime festivals or markets elsewhere on the Treasure Coast.

 When: Saturday, Oct. 3, 5–9 p.m. Where: MIDFLORIDA Event Center, 9221 SE Event Center Place, Port St. Lucie Cost: No price is listed in the TCT event calendar Details: View the TCT event listing 4. Jambush — Vero Beach

 Indian River County's pick for the weekend is Jambush at Riverside Theatre in Vero Beach.

 The Saturday evening performance brings together former members of The String Assassins with Florida musicians for a live show at Riverside Theatre. It is scheduled from 5:30 to 8:30 p.m.

 When: Saturday, Oct. 3, 5:30–8:30 p.m. Where: Riverside Theatre, 3250 Riverside Park Drive, Vero Beach Cost: No price is listed in the TCT event calendar Details: View the TCT event listing 5. Cruzin' to Fall Car Show & '70s Dance Party — Fort Pierce

 Sunday's standout combines a car show with an afternoon of 1970s rock at Summer Crush Vineyard & Winery in Fort Pierce.

 The Cruzin' to Fall event runs from noon to 3 p.m. and pairs the car show with music from Collins & Company, including a salute to Journey, Phil Collins and Genesis. Admission is listed at $6.50.

 When: Sunday, Oct. 4, noon–3 p.m. Where: Summer Crush Vineyard & Winery, 4200 Johnston Road, Fort Pierce Cost: $6.50 Details: View the TCT event listing More things to do

 These are just five of the events happening around the Treasure Coast this weekend. You can browse more local festivals, markets, live music, family activities and community events on the Treasure Coast Today Events Calendar .

cards.headline: Looking for something to do this weekend? Here are the Top 5 local events for Sept. 26-27
cards.teaser: Barbecue, a film festival, rodeo action, classic cars and a Jimmy Buffett tribute are among the top things happening across the Treasure Coast this weekend.
cards.body:
The final weekend of September brings barbecue, live music, movies, classic cars, and a rodeo to communities across the Treasure Coast.

 Here are five events worth checking out Saturday and Sunday, Sept. 26-27.

 Treasure Coast International Film, Arts and Music Festival

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie opens third annual Halloween house decorating contest
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie residents can enter their Halloween displays in the city's third annual Spooktacular House & Yard Decorating Contest beginning Oct. 1.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie residents can show off their Halloween displays this October as the city brings back its Spooktacular House & Yard Decorating Contest for a third year.

 Entries open Oct. 1 at 9 a.m. and close Oct. 29 at midnight. The contest is free to enter and is open to Port St. Lucie residents with exterior Halloween decorations visible from the road.

 Decorations must be kept to a PG-13 rating and cannot obstruct roads or sidewalks. Participants must also agree to allow the city to photograph their displays and publish their addresses online as part of the contest.

 Prizes will be awarded in four categories:

 Classic Halloween Cute n' Creepy — Kid-friendly Halloween decorations Spine Chilling Haunting Light Show — Displays featuring elements such as drones, pixels, projection screens, matrices and other lighting effects Residents can enter by visiting CityofPSL.com/SpookyPSL and selecting the contest entry option.

 Halloween tour and public voting

 Homes entered in the contest will also be added to Port St. Lucie's Spooktacular Halloween Tour Map. The searchable map will include photos and addresses so residents can visit participating displays around the city.

 The city is asking visitors to be courteous when touring neighborhoods and reminds drivers that the residential speed limit in Port St. Lucie neighborhoods is 25 mph.

 Public voting will run from Oct. 30 through Nov. 3. The home receiving the most votes in each category will receive a custom award.

 Winners are scheduled to be announced Nov. 5 on the City of Port St. Lucie's website and social media accounts. Winners will also be recognized at a future City Council meeting.

cards.headline: Donalds, Jolly outline differences on taxes, schools and data centers in Florida race
cards.teaser: Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly outlined different approaches to property-tax revenue, school accountability and data centers in closing interviews as they campai
cards.body:
Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly outlined different approaches to property-tax revenue, school accountability and data centers in closing interviews as they campaigned across Florida. A University of North Florida poll released last week found the governor’s race statistically tied. Donalds, a Republican congressman, wants to build on the policies of outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis, while Jolly, who served in Congress as a Republican during the 2010s, is emphasizing housing, health care and education.

 Donalds supports continuing Florida’s Department of Government Efficiency, which DeSantis created by executive order in 2025 and which has audited multiple counties. He said that work would be important if voters approve Amendment 3, which would raise homestead tax exemptions and reduce local revenue. Donalds said he has committed to a funding formula to help fiscally constrained counties whose budgets would change significantly. Jolly personally opposes the amendment but said he would support voters’ decision if it passes. “I think we all want the math behind Amendment 3 to work, but it just doesn't,” Jolly said.

 Both candidates support keeping universal school vouchers. Jolly also wants greater transparency requirements for charter schools and higher pay for public school teachers. He said schools accepting vouchers should provide the same services, meet the same standards and face the same measures as public schools.

 Asked whether charter school financial records should be public, Donalds emphasized student achievement, including attainment in math and reading, along with ACT and SAT scores. “I think that's the accountability and the transparency that parents are looking for in the state of Florida, because at the end of the day, they're looking to make sure that the output is where it needs to be.”

 The candidates also differ on data center construction. Jolly supports a moratorium, while Donalds said local governments should decide whether to allow the facilities. Donalds said that when local governments approve data centers, the state should protect water resources and ensure utility costs are not passed to consumers.

 Jolly said he wants to work across party lines on his broader agenda, arguing that expanding health care access would reduce costs and that investments in public education and stable housing would strengthen the economy. Donalds also pledged to continue immigration enforcement and expand government-efficiency reviews to local governments and state agencies throughout Florida.

cards.headline: Florida approves USAA auto insurance rate cuts averaging 7% for over 498,000 policies
cards.teaser: Florida Insurance Commissioner Mike Yaworsky has approved USAA Group auto insurance rate reductions averaging 7% across more than 498,000 policies statewide, according to the Flori
cards.body:
Florida Insurance Commissioner Mike Yaworsky has approved USAA Group auto insurance rate reductions averaging 7% across more than 498,000 policies statewide, according to the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation. The approvals cover several auto insurance programs, with savings varying by program.

 Average rate decreases range from 0.4% to 11.2%, according to the state. USAA has its highest concentration of Florida business in Brevard, Escambia and Okaloosa counties. Average reductions in those counties are 5.8% in Brevard, 8% in Escambia and 8.4% in Okaloosa.

 “The Office of Insurance Regulation is constantly reaching out to insurers to inquire about rate relief, and USAA is always stepping up to the plate and looking out for their consumers,” Yaworsky said in a release. He also encouraged other insurers to consider additional rate reductions.

 Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia characterized the reductions as another sign of improvement in the state's insurance market and credited Florida's tort reforms. “These auto insurance rate decreases will help Florida families keep more of their hard-earned money in their pockets, especially our military families,” Ingoglia said.

 The latest approvals follow other savings USAA provided to Florida members over the past year. Between December 2025 and July 2026, the company provided nearly $1 billion in rate reductions and direct member returns, according to the release. That total included a $500 million dividend distributed to approximately 830,000 members.

 State regulators also reported that Florida's five largest auto insurance groups have a combined indicated rate change of negative 12.6% for 2026. Those companies represent 81% of the state's auto insurance market, according to the release. The state also reported that Florida's personal auto liability loss ratio was 52.5% in 2025, the lowest in the nation and Florida's lowest level in 15 years.

cards.headline: ACLU Letter Alleges Abuse, Medical Neglect at 'Deportation Depot' Facility
cards.teaser: The ACLU and other advocacy groups have filed a letter alleging widespread abuse of detainees at the Florida immigration detention facility known as "Deportation Depot." The groups
cards.body:
The ACLU and other advocacy groups have filed a letter alleging widespread abuse of detainees at the Florida immigration detention facility known as "Deportation Depot." The groups say they conducted dozens of interviews with people currently or recently detained at the facility, their loved ones, and attorneys who represent detainees there, and that those interviews point to a pattern of serious abuse.

 The letter identifies seven categories of abuse: life-threatening medical neglect; lack of adequate food and clean drinking water; excessive, life-threatening heat; squalid, unsanitary, and unsafe living conditions; deprivation of necessities for physical, mental, and emotional wellbeing such as sleep, family visitation, and outdoor recreation; verbal and physical abuse and retaliation; and lack of access to the courts and to confidential communication with attorneys. On the issue of food, the letter states that detainees are not given enough nutritious food, describing portions as "extremely small, infant-sized food portions that are not filling" that lack adequate protein or nutrients. It cites cases of dramatic weight loss, including one detainee who lost 29 pounds in less than two months and another who lost 44 pounds over seven months.

 On water, the letter alleges the facility does not provide adequate access to clean drinking water. It says the only water available in the dorms most of the time comes from visibly rusty fountains, and that newly arrived detainees are warned by others not to drink from them because many people have gotten sick doing so. One former detainee named Ryan said he and others would try to drink as much water as possible from the cafeteria during their brief mealtimes because it was the only source of clean water. He said that in the dorms, "you had no alternative sometimes than just to kind of take your chances with the water," describing it as having "a very strong metallic taste" that made his stomach feel like "something was kicking and punching" it once it settled.

 ACLU attorney Amy Godshall, who wrote the letter, said the facility appears designed to strip detainees of basic dignity. "It's very much a cruel facility that's designed to deny people every aspect of humanity and decency and dignity, and is designed to make people physically weak, mentally weak, and just pressured to agree to the point where they agree to self deportation," she said.

 The letter argues this pressure may be intentional, stating there is evidence of a deliberate effort to make detention conditions unbearable so that people give up their legal rights and accept removal, adding that whether or not the conditions are intentional, they are punitive and unconstitutional. Ryan said he was approached by guards on three or four separate occasions and asked to sign forms consenting to his own deportation. "The question that a lot of us had is, well, if we were deportable, then why would we have to sign this document to make us deportable?" he said.

cards.headline: Leon County probe: CBP agents at polling site tried to vote, not enforce
cards.teaser: Leon County election officials and the FBI have concluded that Customs and Border Protection agents seen near an early voting site this week were mistakenly trying to vote before l
cards.body:
Leon County election officials and the FBI have concluded that Customs and Border Protection agents seen near an early voting site this week were mistakenly trying to vote before leaving the state, not conducting an immigration enforcement action. A separate incident involving an armed arrest near a Key Largo polling place remains under review by Monroe County election officials. Both episodes drew scrutiny because federal law bars armed officers or troops from operating near polling places, and the Trump administration has repeatedly assured election officials that federal agents would not be stationed at voting sites.

 The Leon County incident began Monday when two CBP vehicles parked outside the Northeast Branch Library, described by county election supervisor Mark Earley as the busiest early voting site in the county. The vehicles stayed about 10 minutes before leaving. Earley said his office received no calls from voters about the incident, but he filed a complaint with the FBI because voters may experience intimidation.

 On Friday, Earley's office said the county sheriff's office and FBI determined the vehicles belonged to a team of agents normally stationed in south Florida who had been reassigned to another state. While driving north to their new post, they stopped at the last Florida polling place on their route after realizing they would not be in the state on Election Day.

 Earley said the agents mistakenly believed they could vote there, even though they were not Leon County voters, and left immediately once they learned otherwise. He said he accepts that account and considers it an isolated incident consistent with assurances that federal agents would not be stationed at polling sites.

 A CBP spokesperson said the officers were traveling in a government vehicle from Florida to Brownsville, Texas, in support of an out-of-state deployment, and that the stop was not an immigration enforcement action. The officers, who were out of uniform, asked whether they could vote early before leaving the state and were told they were only eligible to vote in their home county. The spokesperson said the officers thanked staff and promptly departed, and that government personnel, like all eligible Americans, may exercise their right to vote.

 The second incident occurred Tuesday outside the Murray Nelson Government Center in Key Largo, where a community group posted video showing masked and armed federal agents conducting what appeared to be a traffic stop near the polling site. A representative of the group 50501 Key Largo said it was unclear why the agents were there and raised concern that their presence could intimidate voters.

 Monroe County election supervisor Sherri Hodies said CBP told her agents were trying to pull over a suspect who turned toward the government center, and her office is investigating. A CBP spokesperson said Border Patrol agents assigned to the Marathon Station stopped a vehicle on U.S. Highway 1 as part of a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Arwiin Pillay, described as a Malaysian national in the country illegally with prior charges for drug possession and battery.

 The spokesperson said the driver pulled into a parking lot adjacent to the polling location, where agents arrested Pillay and left shortly after. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said agents would only be present at polling places if there were a threat to the site or if they were serving a warrant on someone they were actively tracking.

cards.headline: Florida Senate President Albritton Now Opposes Amendment 3
cards.teaser: Florida Senate President Ben Albritton says he will vote against Amendment 3 in November, months after the State Senate voted to place the measure on the ballot. Amendment 3 would
cards.body:
Florida Senate President Ben Albritton says he will vote against Amendment 3 in November, months after the State Senate voted to place the measure on the ballot. Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption for Florida homeowners to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and would cut property taxes for homesteaded homeowners, excluding school taxes. The measure needs 60% voter approval on Election Day to become law.

 Albritton announced his opposition in a post on the Florida Sheriffs Association's Instagram page. "As a native of Florida's Heartland, our rural communities are near and dear to my heart," Albritton said. "Amendment 3 would eliminate up to 30% of resources for Florida's rural counties, gutting essential support for law enforcement, emergency response services and critical infrastructure."

 Albritton pointed to the Florida Taxation and Budget Reform Commission as a better avenue for change, calling it "an ideal opportunity to design property tax reform and create a solution that is meaningful, reasonable and balanced."

 Cities and counties across Florida stand to lose significant revenue if the amendment passes. Local leaders have warned it could force budget cuts, reduce services, and push governments to find other sources of revenue.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds Brings Governor Bus Tour to Fort Pierce College Campus
cards.teaser: Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds stopped at Indian River State College's Eastman Workforce Center in Fort Pierce, joined by Congressman Brian Mast and State Senator Erin Grall to rally voters ahead of election day.
cards.body:
Republican gubernatorial candidate and Congressman Byron Donalds stopped in Fort Pierce on Tuesday as part of a statewide bus tour, holding a campaign event at Indian River State College's Eastman Workforce Center. Donalds was joined by his running mate for lieutenant governor, Bryan Avila, along with Congressman Brian Mast and State Senator Erin Grall, as the group worked to drive voter turnout in the final stretch before election day.

 "I think for us we're just focused on making sure we drive turnout to the polls," Donalds said.

 The Fort Pierce stop came in the middle of Tuesday's leg of the bus tour, which began in Melbourne and later continued to Miami. Donalds and Avila held a meet and greet in front of the campaign bus outside the Eastman Workforce Center, taking photos and talking with supporters who gathered at the stop.

 "We show up, we stand outside, we take pictures with you, sign the bus, we have conversations with the voters. We've been consistently doing that for months now on the campaign trail. We're going to continue to do it every single day. I think the symbolism of the bus tour, it just helps people know that you're out here working hard for their vote and you want their support," Donalds said.

 Donalds also laid out the economic message he has carried throughout the campaign, telling the Fort Pierce crowd that affordability for families and seniors remains central to his pitch to voters.

 "We want our kids to achieve the Florida dream for themselves. We want to make sure it's affordable for our seniors and our working families in our state. That's what we've been laser focused on this entire time. We haven't gotten off of that," Donalds said.

hero.headline: Murray Middle School breaks ground on $33 million rebuild after tornado damage
hero.teaser: Murray Middle School has broken ground on a $33 million rebuilding phase that will add permanent learning and performing arts spaces after a tornado spawned by Hurricane Milton dam
hero.body:
Murray Middle School has broken ground on a $33 million rebuilding phase that will add permanent learning and performing arts spaces after a tornado spawned by Hurricane Milton damaged three main buildings and forced students into portable classrooms. School officials expect gym renovations to be completed by August 2027 and the new buildings to be finished by December 2027.

 Students and staff gathered for the groundbreaking as the school moves into the second phase of its campus rebuilding project. The work includes a performing arts wing with band and choir rooms, new learning spaces and gym renovations. Murray Middle School Principal Tiffany Roth said students will also have a new media center, an art room and an agriculture room.

 Martin County Superintendent Michael Maine said campus improvements were planned before Hurricane Milton, but the storm damage added urgency. About $33 million has been approved for the second phase, according to school officials. “When Hurricane Milton came through and spawned the tornado, it took down three of our main buildings that we rely on every single day,” Maine said. “We couldn't have our students displaced in portables any longer than we needed to.”

 Choir was among the programs forced out of permanent space by the storm. Dr. Anita Caswell, Murray Middle School's choir and drama director, said the damage destroyed decades of program materials, including costumes and props. “It was 60 years of drama props,” Caswell said. “Our dresses were in that, the boys' vest that we used to sing in, and just to see it all mangled and stuck up on the wall, it just hurt.”

 Caswell said students continued singing in a portable classroom and earned straight superior ratings that year. Murray Middle student Nicholas Lowe said the move required him to adjust to a different learning environment. Roth said she hopes students take pride in being Murray Lions and enjoy the new buildings when they are finished.

cards.headline: Mattamy Homes transferring 125 acres in Martin County for St. Lucie River muck storage
cards.teaser: Mattamy Homes is transferring 125 acres to Martin County to store muck dredged from the St. Lucie River as part of efforts to improve water quality. The removal project will begin
cards.body:
Mattamy Homes is transferring 125 acres to Martin County to store muck dredged from the St. Lucie River as part of efforts to improve water quality. The removal project will begin once federal funding is authorized, a company official said.

 The parcel is in the northern section of the Newfield development. The developer said the land was donated to the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan, a federal plan to restore, protect and preserve South Florida's water resources.

 James Fitzgerald, vice president of community development for Mattamy Homes Southeast Florida Division, said the Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) is also donating an adjacent 125 acres. Together, the 250 acres can hold 2.4 million cubic yards of muck removed from the river, Fitzgerald said.

 Fitzgerald said the muck will dry out after removal. He expressed hope that the land could eventually be used for recreation or, depending on the county's needs, other environmental restoration projects.

cards.headline: 15-year-old and other driver seriously hurt in U.S. 1 crash near Treasure Coast Square Mall
cards.teaser: Stuart police say the fleeing driver in Tuesday’s wrong-way crash near Treasure Coast Square Mall was 15 years old. The teen and the other driver suffered serious injuries and were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center in Fort Pierce.
cards.body:
An Audi SUV traveling the wrong way during a police pursuit struck an oncoming vehicle Tuesday on U.S. 1 near Treasure Coast Square Mall, closing all southbound lanes. Stuart police now say the fleeing driver was 15 years old and that both drivers suffered serious injuries. Both were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center in Fort Pierce after the collision at the Mall South Entrance intersection.

 The pursuit began after officers conducting traffic enforcement near Southwest Federal Highway and Southwest St. Lucie Crescent spotted a vehicle traveling north at what they described as an extremely high rate of speed around 3:45 a.m. An officer attempted a traffic stop, but the driver refused to stop and fled, according to the Stuart Police Department.

 Police said the pursuit continued onto U.S. 1, where the fleeing driver began traveling north in the southbound lanes from Wright Boulevard. Officers continued trying to stop the vehicle because of the danger to other motorists and also tried to alert drivers traveling on Northwest Federal Highway, according to police.

 The fleeing vehicle then collided with a southbound vehicle at the mall entrance intersection. Officers learned after the crash that the fleeing driver was 15. Authorities previously said the pursuit involved Stuart Police and the Martin County Sheriff’s Office.

 The southbound lanes of U.S. 1 reopened around 7:58 a.m. The Stuart Police Department is investigating the incident, while the Florida Highway Patrol is conducting a separate investigation into the crash.

cards.headline: Arrest report details speeding, 0.246 blood-alcohol level in deputy's Vero Beach crash
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County sheriff’s deputy Tyler Horstman, arrested Monday on a felony DUI charge tied to a March 1 crash in Vero Beach, was driving 63 mph in a 35 mph zone and had a blood-
cards.body:
St. Lucie County sheriff’s deputy Tyler Horstman, arrested Monday on a felony DUI charge tied to a March 1 crash in Vero Beach, was driving 63 mph in a 35 mph zone and had a blood-alcohol level of 0.246, according to police and his arrest report. The woman driving the other vehicle suffered a traumatic brain injury, the report says. Horstman turned himself in Monday afternoon after a felony warrant was issued, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office.

 The crash happened about 11:25 p.m. at Beachland Boulevard and A1A. Horstman was off duty and driving an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office pickup truck when he struck a Chevy Equinox carrying the woman and an infant, according to the arrest report. Vero Beach police said Horstman entered the intersection on a green light and the other driver entered against a red light.

 Both drivers were injured and taken to the hospital. The infant was alert and responsive, according to the report.

 The arrest report says Horstman stated he had a few beers earlier in the evening. It describes a “faint odor of alcohol on his breath” and says he was “lethargic and dazed” and “drowsy and periodically dozing off.” The Sheriff’s Office received his blood-test results on September 9. His blood-alcohol concentration of 0.246 was more than three times Florida’s legal limit. Horstman was placed on administrative leave on September 15.

 The felony warrant issued Monday lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. Horstman was booked into the Indian River County Jail at 4:59 p.m. and posted $15,000 bond at 6:24 p.m. His arraignment is scheduled for December 9.

 Vero Beach police are leading the criminal investigation, according to the Sheriff’s Office. The agency’s internal investigation is on hold pending the outcome of the criminal case.

cards.headline: Man arrested after reported disturbance on Crooked Oak Avenue in Hobe Sound
cards.teaser: Joseph Oswald, 28, faces loitering, prowling and trespassing charges after residents called 911, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.
cards.body:
Joseph Oswald, 28, was arrested after residents along the 6000 block of Crooked Oak Avenue in Hobe Sound called 911 to report suspicious activity, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Deputies said he was yelling at people and wandering through the neighborhood.

 Responding deputies found Oswald appearing to be under the influence of an unknown substance, the sheriff's office said. He faces charges of loitering, prowling and trespassing.

 Oswald had been released from prison 11 days earlier. According to the sheriff's office, he has had as many as 14 prior arrests in Martin County on charges ranging from grand theft and burglary to loitering and prowling. The sheriff's office praised residents for quickly reporting the activity, saying community members play an important role in keeping their neighborhoods safe by reporting suspicious behavior.

hero.headline: State review finds St. Lucie County glioblastoma cases in line with expectations
hero.teaser: A new Florida Department of Health review found 95 glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County from 2019 through 2023, compared with 92 expected, a difference officials say is not stati
hero.body:
A new Florida Department of Health review found 95 glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County from 2019 through 2023, compared with 92 expected, a difference officials say is not statistically significant. The analysis examined countywide totals rather than concentrations on individual streets or in specific neighborhoods, leaving families’ concerns about geographic patterns unresolved. The findings largely match the conclusion of the state’s 2019 investigation into cases of the aggressive brain cancer.

 Clint Sperber, administrator for the Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County, said the latest findings remain consistent with statewide expectations for the county. Officials also reviewed existing water and radiation monitoring records without identifying new concerns. The latest analysis presents countywide totals without age or sex breakdowns because officials said the number of cases was too small to make those comparisons statistically reliable. The 2019 investigation had included those breakdowns and examined environmental monitoring information, including public water utility data and radiation monitoring records associated with the area’s power plant.

 Families’ concerns have centered on both the ages of some patients and how close they lived to one another. Some patients lived within blocks of each other or on the same street. In one instance, unrelated patients had lived in the same home.

 Glioblastoma is most commonly diagnosed in older adults, but local patients included Lenny Schelin Jr., who died at 33, Mark Cunningham, who was in his 30s, and Kyle Vericella, who was 18. Schelin survived 17 months after his diagnosis. His mother, Deb Johnston, wants investigators to examine individual neighborhoods more closely, particularly the White City area.

 Nearly eight years after her son’s death, Johnston remains grateful that health officials continue to review the cases, but she is still seeking answers. “I haven't given up, it's just you get tired,” she said. She hosts an annual fishing tournament honoring Schelin, who loved fishing, and the event has raised nearly $300,000 for glioblastoma research. The Florida Department of Health has invested at least $9 million in research into the disease. Sperber said identifying a single environmental cause is difficult, pointing to research identifying nearly a dozen potential factors associated with glioblastoma.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested, accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger
cards.teaser: Investigators say Anthony Pizzarelli demanded an apology and support for government audits, including in St. Lucie County. He denied using his communications as leverage.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he tried to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger by threatening lawsuits and ethics complaints unless she publicly apologized and supported government audits, including in St. Lucie County. The allegations against Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, are outlined in a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office probable cause affidavit.

 Pizzarelli faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. He told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he wanted an apology over an incident involving an email on which she had been copied and was seeking her support for his complaints. He is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

 Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9, offering to leave her out of planned lawsuits and ethics complaints if she issued a swift public apology. He proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, he wanted audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and investigations into government contracting.

 The affidavit says Pizzarelli sent a voice memo directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone on May 18, 2026. Among his statements were “I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice,” and “you don't know what I can do.” Weinberger told investigators she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family's safety. A first-term Republican, she represents Florida House District 94, which is entirely within Palm Beach County.

 In 2025, Pizzarelli was arrested after being accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies said the communications escalated in tone and content, raising concern among officials. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from that case had been dropped.

 Weinberger's campaign also faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election involving Nicholas Farley, not Pizzarelli. cards.body:
St. Lucie County sheriff’s deputy Tyler Horstman, arrested Monday on a felony DUI charge tied to a March 1 crash in Vero Beach, was driving 63 mph in a 35 mph zone and had a blood-alcohol level of 0.246, according to police and his arrest report. The woman driving the other vehicle suffered a traumatic brain injury, the report says. Horstman turned himself in Monday afternoon after a felony warrant was issued, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office.

 The crash happened about 11:25 p.m. at Beachland Boulevard and A1A. Horstman was off duty and driving an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office pickup truck when he struck a Chevy Equinox carrying the woman and an infant, according to the arrest report. Vero Beach police said Horstman entered the intersection on a green light and the other driver entered against a red light.

 Both drivers were injured and taken to the hospital. The infant was alert and responsive, according to the report.

 The arrest report says Horstman stated he had a few beers earlier in the evening. It describes a “faint odor of alcohol on his breath” and says he was “lethargic and dazed” and “drowsy and periodically dozing off.” The Sheriff’s Office received his blood-test results on September 9. His blood-alcohol concentration of 0.246 was more than three times Florida’s legal limit. Horstman was placed on administrative leave on September 15.

 The felony warrant issued Monday lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. cards.headline: Fort Pierce Police: Missing 5-Year-Old Found Dead in Pond Near Portofino Landing
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police say a 5-year-old nonverbal girl who went missing from her apartment complex Saturday was found dead hours later in a nearby pond, with investigators now revealin
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police say a 5-year-old nonverbal girl who went missing from her apartment complex Saturday was found dead hours later in a nearby pond, with investigators now revealing new details about the search effort, including an attempt to track her location through a tablet she had with her. Mayra Glory Odelus was last seen before noon in the 5100 block of Portofino Landing Apartments east of Interstate 95.

 Her body was discovered in the pond at about 3 p.m., roughly 75 yards from her apartment, about three hours after she was reported missing. Police received the initial report at 11:39 a.m., and family members told officers Mayra was autistic and nonverbal.

 She was last seen wearing a dark oversized shirt with two white beads in her hair. Officers searched the surrounding area, handed out flyers with her name and photo, and flew drones over the area. Police called in Port St. Lucie bloodhounds and the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office dive team, which conducted an underwater search that led to the discovery of her body.

 According to police spokesperson Michael Santiago, Mayra had a tablet with her when she disappeared, and her family tried to locate her by pinging the device. The ping led searchers to the pond area, but at that point there was no sign of her, and the tablet itself has still not been recovered.

 Mayra's father told police the pond sits directly across from their apartment and that she loved the water. He and Mayra's 18-year-old sister were home at the time she went missing. Her mother lives in Haiti and was expected to arrive Sunday.

 "Our deepest condolences are with Mayra's family and loved ones during this tragic time," the Fort Pierce Police Department said in a statement. Santiago added, "It's very tragic when anything like this happens, but with our kids we have to make sure we're paying attention all the time, especially when kids are challenged with autism."

 Drowning remains the leading cause of unintentional death among children ages 1 to 3. Dr. Elizabeth Feldman of Cleveland Clinic Florida has said drowning can happen within seconds, and a lack of oxygen for just a few minutes can cause brain injury. The Children's Services Council of Palm Beach reported that 39 children with autism or suspected autism drowned in Florida in 2025, the highest number ever recorded in the state. The case has renewed attention on tracking and safety devices designed to prevent or respond to water-related emergencies involving children with autism, many of whom are drawn to water and may wander from supervision without being able to call for help.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Firefighter-Paramedic Austin Hodge Dies in Line of Duty
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge died while on duty Oct. 24, about 15 months after his brother Jarius, also a firefighter. The district and fellow first responders are mourning his death.
cards.body:
The siblings of St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge are seeking answers about his death after the 34-year-old died while on duty Oct. 24. His siblings, Alexis Hodge and Javan Hodge, want to understand what happened in his final hours and what caused his death.

 Alexis said the family was told Austin appeared to be himself before going to bed. He had been cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes, according to the account relayed to them. “Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said. Alexis and Javan gathered at Austin’s home and remembered him as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others. Along with his work as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin worked as a respiratory therapist, his family said.

 Austin’s death came just over a year after the death of his younger brother, Jairus “Jay” Hodge, 26, who also served with the fire district. The family said Jairus became sick while on shift in July 2025 and later died. They raised concerns about the medical care Jairus received and said Austin sought answers and advocated for his brother. “He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it,” Javan said. “He would not rest until he could spread Jay’s legacy globally.”

 Now, Alexis and Javan are seeking answers about Austin. “I want to know A to Z what happened,” Javan said. Alexis said they want to establish who was around Austin and who saw him before he was found unresponsive. “After I get my answers, then I can rest and heal from my grief,” she said.

 Both siblings said they are determined to make Austin and Jairus proud. Javan said Austin inspired him to pursue a career in healthcare. He is studying to become a nurse and preparing to graduate in December. “I do know I want to make him proud.

 I do know I want to make both of my brothers proud,” Javan said. “The love I have for them is unimaginable. It has no bounds.”

hero.headline: Erosion hits Ocean Drive beachfront parking in Vero Beach as king tides persist
hero.teaser: Coastal erosion caused by king tides and strong onshore winds has affected a section of beachfront parking on Ocean Drive in Vero Beach, prompting officials to contact park officia
hero.body:
Coastal erosion caused by king tides and strong onshore winds has affected a section of beachfront parking on Ocean Drive in Vero Beach, prompting officials to contact park officials about public safety measures. The area is one of the erosion hot spots officials have identified along the coast.

 Quintin Bergman, the resource manager with Indian River County, is monitoring the damage along the Vero Beach boardwalk. He said the erosion is approaching severe as the two weather events continue to affect the shoreline. “I would classify this as leaning more on the severe side of erosion. It's not extreme by any means, but definitely we are very concerned,” Bergman said.

 The forecast calls for elevated winds for a few more days, and king tides will continue to affect the water level, Bergman said. “We're still in the middle of this. We're not through with the weather event. The forecast is showing elevated winds for a few more days, and the king tide event is still going to be affecting the tide.” Officials plan to assess the damage after the weather event passes.

 Beachgoers have also noticed changes to the shoreline. Svetlana Ryan was among those still enjoying the view in Vero Beach despite the erosion. “We noticed because there was so much sand before, and now it's just a wall. But you do with whatever you have to do here in Vero Beach,” Ryan said.

cards.headline: Indian River County sets record with 14,083 turtle nests as rough surf threatens eggs
cards.teaser: Decades of conservation helped Indian River County reach its highest nest count. Rough surf and king tides now threaten remaining nests and have delayed damage surveys.
cards.body:
Indian River County recorded a record 14,083 sea turtle nests as of Oct. 22, while rough surf and king tides threaten remaining nests and have delayed surveys to assess damage. The total surpassed the county’s previous record, set in 2023, by approximately 2,000 nests, according to Coastal Specialist Dakota Whalen. Loggerheads accounted for 10,045 nests, followed by 3,970 green turtle nests and 68 leatherback nests. Whalen said loggerheads drove much of the increase that pushed the county to its highest recorded total.

 Whalen credited decades of conservation work for the milestone, including monitoring, partnerships with conservation groups and efforts to encourage turtle-friendly beach practices. Along the county’s 22.4-mile coastline, orange markers identify approximately one in 10 nests. Researchers evaluate those marked nests to help measure reproductive success.

 The markers beachgoers see represent only a fraction of the nesting activity. Whalen said marking all 14,000 nests would leave beachgoers little room to sit. The long-term gains reflect years of work protecting both sea turtles and their nesting beaches, he said.

 A nor’easter and king tides have brought powerful waves and high water as nesting season winds down. Waves strip sand from the beach, potentially exposing buried eggs, and unsafe conditions have delayed surveys needed to determine the full extent of the damage. Whalen estimated that 75% to 90% of the county’s nests had already hatched before the recent rough weather. Indian River County’s nesting season officially ends on Halloween, though some nests may continue incubating beyond that date.

 The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission advises beachgoers to leave exposed eggs in place rather than collect or rebury them. Eggs swept from their nests rarely survive. Storm currents can also carry young turtles ashore, sometimes tangled in seaweed.

 These washback turtles may need specialized care. People should not pick them up or return them to the ocean, but should immediately call FWC’s 24-hour Wildlife Alert Hotline at 888-404-3922 for instructions. Hatchlings actively crawling toward the ocean do not need assistance. Beachgoers can help keep nesting beaches clean, flat and dark by removing beach gear, filling holes, flattening sandcastles and keeping lights off the beach at night.

cards.headline: 86-Year-Old Found Dead After Car Plunges Into Indian River Lagoon in Vero Beach

cards.body:
An 86-year-old man was found dead inside a car pulled from the Indian River Lagoon in Vero Beach after witnesses said the vehicle drove through a fence at a condo complex and into the water. Police have not yet identified the man. Authorities said he had gone missing the night before the car was discovered.

 Residents at the condo complex said they knew the driver. Tire marks were visible near the scene where the car breached the fence before entering the lagoon. Police worked for hours to pull the silver Honda CR-V from the water as the investigation got underway.

 The crash left a visible mark on the community. Residents on Greytwig Road were later seen cleaning up the parking lot, removing mud and scrubbing away tire marks left behind. Several described the scene as unsettling.

 Police have not released the identity of the victim and continue to investigate what led up to the crash. The case remains active as authorities work to determine the circumstances that caused the vehicle to leave the roadway and enter the lagoon.
